a-theory.definition: The A-theory holds that past, present, and future are objectively different and that time really passes. The B-theory holds that all times are equally real and that 'now' is like 'here', a matter of perspective.

antinomy.definition: Kant's name for a pair of opposite conclusions that reason seems able to prove equally well when it overreaches, for example that the world had a beginning and that it did not.

axiopistic.definition: Gary Phillips's name for an apologetic strategy that argues from standards believers and unbelievers share.

bccf.definition: The conjunction of all contingent truths, used in van Inwagen's argument against the full Principle of Sufficient Reason.

brute fact.definition: A fact with no explanation at all: not hidden, not merely unknown, but absent.

contingent.definition: A contingent fact is one that could have been otherwise. A necessary fact could not have been otherwise.

creatio ex nihilo.definition: Latin for 'creation out of nothing.' The doctrine that God brought the universe into being with no pre-existing material.

defeasible reasoning.definition: Reasoning to conclusions that hold by default but can be overturned by further information.

efficient cause.definition: That which produces an effect. Michelangelo was the efficient cause of the David.

eliminativism.definition: The view that causation is not part of fundamental reality and that causal talk is only an approximation.

entropy.definition: A measure of disorder. The second law of thermodynamics says it tends to increase, and many philosophers of physics think that increase is what gives time its direction.

ex nihilo nihil fit.definition: Latin for 'out of nothing, nothing comes.' The principle that nothing begins to exist with no cause or explanation whatsoever.

folk science.definition: Norton's term for a body of useful rules of thumb that work in everyday domains but have no place in fundamental theory.

folk theory.definition: A rule of thumb ordinary people live by, which experts expect to retire.

hinge.definition: In Wittgenstein's On Certainty, a proposition that frames inquiry rather than being tested by it.

induction.definition: Reasoning from observed cases to a general rule: every observed beginning has had a cause, so probably all beginnings do.

material cause.definition: That out of which a thing is made. The block of Carrara marble was the material cause of the David.

mentaculus.definition: David Albert and Barry Loewer's name for statistical-mechanical laws together with a postulate that the universe began in a low-entropy state, which fix the probabilities of everything after.

metaphysical possibility.definition: What could really be the case given the natures of things. Stricter than logical possibility, broader than physical possibility.

modal collapse.definition: The result that every truth is a necessary truth, leaving no room for anything to have been otherwise.

normalizable.definition: A probability measure is normalizable if the probabilities can be made to add up to one. Spread evenly over an infinite space, they cannot.

psr.definition: Every contingent fact has an explanation for why it is true.

reductio.definition: Refuting a claim by showing that it leads to something absurd.

reify.definition: From the Latin res, 'thing.' To treat an abstraction or an absence as though it were a thing.

statistical mechanics.definition: The branch of physics that explains the behavior of large systems, like a gas, from the probabilities governing their microscopic parts.

tautology.definition: In the Tractatus, a proposition that is true whatever the world is like. Logic consists of them, so it shows the structure of description and says nothing about which world exists.

verification principle.definition: The logical positivist claim that a statement is meaningful only if logic or experience can check it.
